stem: A review agent treats every issue as equally important — trivial style nits flagged as loudly as security bugs. What most improves this?

options.label: A
options.body: Add 2–3 severity-calibration examples showing what counts as critical vs. minor, with specific code samples.
options.rationale: Correct. Without calibration examples the model can't tell critical from minor. Concrete severity examples teach the distinction.

options.label: B
options.body: Tell the agent in prose to 'prioritize the important issues' and leave it to judge on its own which ones actually qualify as important.
options.rationale: Vague prose doesn't define your bar; calibration examples do.

options.label: C
options.body: Switch the review agent to a larger, more capable model tier in the hope that it starts prioritizing serious issues over trivial ones by itself.
options.rationale: Capability isn't the gap — the model doesn't know your severity scale.

options.label: D
options.body: Have the agent only report the very first issue it finds in each file and stay silent about everything else it detects there.
options.rationale: That drops real issues instead of ranking them by severity.

stem: A developer plans to add 12 few-shot examples to squeeze out more extraction quality. What does the guidance say?

options.label: A
options.body: 2–4 examples is the sweet spot; going from 4 to 8+ rarely improves quality and adds context cost.
options.rationale: Correct. The 0→2 jump has the largest impact; diminishing returns set in after ~4. Cover edge cases and include reasoning rather than piling on examples.

options.label: B
options.body: More examples are always better, so a set of 12 few-shot examples will reliably beat a smaller set of just 3.
options.rationale: Diminishing returns: 10+ examples rarely help and cost more context.

options.label: C
options.body: Few-shot examples should generally be avoided in production extraction prompts in order to keep them as lean as possible.
options.rationale: Few-shot is a core technique for consistency; the point is 2–4, not zero.

options.label: D
options.body: Only ever use a single example so that the extraction prompt stays as short and inexpensive as it possibly can.
options.rationale: One example may not cover edge cases; 2–4 is the sweet spot.

stem: You need the response to match one specific JSON structure every single time. What's the exam's preferred pattern?

options.label: A
options.body: Define a tool whose purpose is to structure the output and force it with tool_choice { type: "tool", name: ... }.
options.rationale: Correct. Forced tool_choice guarantees the call, and the tool's JSON schema is validated by the API — no malformed/missing/extra fields.

options.label: B
options.body: Ask for the JSON structure in the prompt and parse whatever the model returns afterward in your own code.
options.rationale: Prompt-based JSON has no schema enforcement — risks malformed output. Use forced tool_choice for production.

options.label: C
options.body: Use tool_choice: auto and simply hope that the model chooses to call the structuring tool on each request it gets.
options.rationale: `auto` may reply with text instead — no guarantee.

options.label: D
options.body: Lower the temperature all the way to 0 so the JSON the model produces comes out deterministic from one run to the next.
options.rationale: Determinism doesn't enforce a schema; the shape can still be wrong.

stem: To stop the model returning null for an important field, a developer makes it `required`. Now the model outputs plausible-but-fabricated values when the data is absent. What's the correct fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Make the field nullable/optional and instruct the model to return null when the value isn't stated.
options.rationale: Correct. Required fields CAUSE fabrication — the model invents a value to satisfy the schema. Nullable fields give it permission to return null.

options.label: B
options.body: Keep the field marked required but add stricter downstream validation rules that reject values which look fabricated.
options.rationale: Required-ness is the cause; stricter validation on a required field just rejects the fabrication after the fact.

options.label: C
options.body: Upgrade to a more capable model in the hope that a stronger one stops fabricating values for data the source doesn't contain.
options.rationale: The schema, not the model, is forcing invention.

options.label: D
options.body: Add a post-processing LLM call that verifies each extracted value against the source document before it is accepted.
options.rationale: Expensive second pass for something the schema design fixes directly.

stem: An extraction fails validation. What should a retry-with-error-feedback message contain?

options.label: A
options.body: The original prompt, the failed output, and the specific validation error.
options.rationale: Correct. Showing what it produced and exactly what was wrong lets the model correct specifically. Never just say 'try again'.

options.label: B
options.body: Just say 'try again' and trust the model to work out on its own what went wrong the first time.
options.rationale: Without the specific error the model can't target the fix.

options.label: C
options.body: A fresh prompt with no reference to the prior attempt.
options.rationale: Dropping the failed output and error loses the signal needed to correct.

options.label: D
options.body: The full document re-pasted with no error details.
options.rationale: More input without the error diagnosis doesn't guide correction.

stem: Processing a large multi-file input in one pass, the model keeps missing details. What's the recommended approach?

options.label: A
options.body: Per-file passes (analyze each file independently) plus a cross-file integration pass to synthesize.
options.rationale: Correct. This mitigates attention dilution — one giant pass causes the model to miss details; focused per-file passes plus an integration pass preserve fidelity.

options.label: B
options.body: Cram every one of the files into a single larger context window and process all of them together in one pass.
options.rationale: One big pass is exactly what dilutes attention and drops details.

options.label: C
options.body: Summarize each file first and then process only those summaries rather than the full contents of the files.
options.rationale: Pre-summaries lose the detail the task needs.

options.label: D
options.body: Review the extracted output in the very same session that originally produced it from the multi-file input.
options.rationale: Same-session review is biased; and it doesn't address the missed-detail problem.
